content: Lavandula angustifolia, also known as Lavandula spica or Lavandula vera, is commonly referred to as Common Lavender, True Lavender, or, inaccurately, English Lavender. Historically, it was also known as L. officinalis. This plant belongs to the Lamiaceae family and is native to the western Mediterranean region, particularly the Pyrenees and other mountainous areas in northern Spain. Despite its common name, it is not native to England. This species is a highly aromatic shrub that typically grows to a height of 1 to 2 meters. Its leaves are evergreen, measuring 2 to 6 cm in length and 4 to 6 mm in width. The flowers are pinkish-purple, often described as lavender-colored, and are borne on spikes that are 2 to 8 cm long. These spikes are located at the tips of slender, leafless stems that range from 10 to 30 cm in length. Cultivation Lavandula angustifolia is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant due to its vibrant flowers, pleasant fragrance, and ability to thrive with minimal water requirements. However, it does not perform well in continuously damp soil. The plant is relatively cold-hardy and is generally considered suitable for USDA hardiness zone 5. Uses In addition to its ornamental value, the flowers and leaves of Lavandula angustifolia are utilized in herbal medicine. They are commonly processed into lavender oil or brewed as herbal tea. The flowers are also used as a culinary herb, most notably as a component of the French herb blend known as herbes de Provence. Lavender essential oil, when diluted with a carrier oil, is frequently employed in massage therapy as a relaxant. Various lavender-based products, such as lotions, eye pillows filled with lavender flowers or infused with essential oil, and bath oils, are also used to promote relaxation and stress relief.
